name: Swarnakadeswarar (Vennaiyappar) Temple, Tirunelvennai
deity: Shiva as Swarnakadeswarar (Vennaiyappar), with the goddess Neelamalar Kanni Ammai
period: Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple raised and renewed in later centuries
summary: Swarnakadeswarar, the Vennaiyappar of Tirunelvennai, is a Shiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country praised by Sambandar in the Tevaram, where the Lord is worshipped as a swayambhu linga sheltered beneath a canopy fashioned of rudraksha beads.

sections.history: Tirunelvennai, the village of Neivanai in the Villupuram country east of Tirukkovilur, is among the Shiva shrines of the Nadu Nadu region sung in the Tevaram, and so is counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam. In the hymns the place is remembered as Nelvennai, an ancient and celebrated land, and tradition names it the tenth of the Nadu Nadu temples praised by the child-saint Tirugnana Sambandar, who honoured it in a decad of the third Tirumurai. The Lord of the shrine is called Swarnakadeswarar in Sanskrit and Vennaiyappar in Tamil, and the goddess is worshipped as Neelamalar Kanni Ammai. Temple tradition holds that the Sanakadi Rishis, the mind-born sages, once worshipped the Lord here, though this belongs to local lore rather than textual record. Raised in stone by later patrons of the Tamil country, the shrine has been kept in worship across the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is small in scale and quiet in feeling, in keeping with the village shrines of the Nadu Nadu country. In the sanctum the Lord is worshipped as a swayambhu linga, held to be self-manifested rather than installed by human hands, and above it rises a canopy wrought in the likeness of rudraksha beads, the dark seeds sacred to Shiva — the feature for which the shrine is best remembered. The goddess Neelamalar Kanni Ammai is honoured in her own sanctum within the enclosure, and before the Lord stand the flagstaff, the offering-pedestal, and the mounted Nandi, as at every Tamil Shiva temple. It is told that at Maha Shivaratri the rays of the sun reach the sanctum and fall upon the Lord, a meeting of light and stone that draws devotees to the festival.
sections.legends: The Sanskrit name Swarnakadeswarar is read as the Lord who bestowed the golden pot, and temple tradition traces the name to an old inscription of the shrine, though the account has not been confirmed against a published source. The story most dear to the place is that of the Sanakadi Rishis, the four mind-born sons of Brahma, who are said to have halted at Nelvennai and worshipped the swayambhu linga, drawn by its sanctity. From these threads the shrine keeps the sense of a very old and self-arisen holiness, a place where the Lord revealed himself of his own accord and the sages came to honour him.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great night of the temple, kept with the vigil and worship observed at every Shiva shrine, and remembered here for the sun's rays said to reach the Lord. The monthly Pradosham is honoured at dusk, and the Shaiva round of the Tamil year — among them Tirukarthikai with its lamps and the Arudra Darshan of winter — is kept as the village observes them. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally before setting out.
sections.experience: Tirunelvennai rewards a quiet, unhurried visit, away from the pilgrim crowds of the larger shrines. Come before the swayambhu linga beneath its canopy of rudraksha, pause to take in a sanctity the hymns have honoured for more than a thousand years, and turn to the goddess Neelamalar Kanni Ammai in her own shrine. The temple keeps the stillness of a small country sanctuary, and devotees who make the journey through the fields east of Tirukkovilur find in it the unhurried devotion of the older Tamil land.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday break, as at most village shrines; confirm timings locally before visiting, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunelvennai lies in Villupuram district, on the road between Tirukkovilur and Ulundurpet by way of Eraiyur and Elavanasur. Ulundurpet and Tirukkovilur are the nearest towns, with bus connections, and Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction. As the village is off the main highways, a local vehicle is the easiest way to reach the temple.
